# Introduction

This analysis examines long-term movements, seasonal patterns,
and variability in monthly Northern Hemisphere surface temperature
anomalies from GISTEMP.

We first explore the observed series and compare classical additive
and multiplicative decompositions. We then use STL to examine
fixed and time-varying seasonal specifications, interpreting the
estimated trend, seasonal component, and remainder.

The forecasting analysis compares simple exponential smoothing
and Holt's method using observations from January 1950 to
December 2010. Seasonal adjustment for this stage is estimated using only
observations dated within the training period.

Forecasts from the end of 2010 are evaluated against subsequent
observations over 2011–2025. We report prediction intervals and
cumulative mean absolute errors over the first 1, 5, 10, and
15 years after the forecast origin.

The analysis describes statistical patterns and the performance
of extrapolative forecasting methods; it does not identify the
physical causes of temperature changes.

# Data Preparation

The dataset contains monthly Northern Hemisphere land–ocean
temperature anomalies relative to the 1951–1980 reference period,
expressed in degrees Celsius.

Each row represents a calendar year. We extract the twelve monthly
columns, excluding annual and seasonal summaries, and arrange the
observations chronologically in a monthly time series.

```{r data-import}
data_url <- paste0(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/",
  "MnGianmaria/time-series-analysis/main/",
  "02_temperature_anomalies_and_forecasting/",
  "data/gistemp.csv"
)

gistemp_raw <- read.csv(
  data_url,
  skip = 1,
  header = TRUE,
  na.strings = "***",
  check.names = FALSE
)

month_names <- c(
  "Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
  "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"
)

monthly_mat <- as.matrix(gistemp_raw[, month_names])
temp_vec <- as.numeric(t(monthly_mat))

stopifnot(
  all(diff(gistemp_raw$Year) == 1),
  all(is.finite(temp_vec))
)

gistemp_ts <- ts(
  temp_vec,
  start = c(gistemp_raw$Year[1], 1),
  frequency = 12
)

gistemp_df <- data.frame(
  date = as.Date(as.yearmon(time(gistemp_ts))),
  value = as.numeric(gistemp_ts)
)
```

The sample covers January 1880 to December 2025, with 1,752 monthly
observations and no missing monthly values. Negative anomalies
indicate temperatures below the reference-period average for the
corresponding calendar month; positive anomalies indicate
temperatures above it.

# Temperature Dynamics

We examine the monthly anomalies to identify long-term movements
and short-term fluctuations.

```{r temperature-series, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=2, out.width="95%", fig.pos="H", fig.cap="Monthly Northern Hemisphere land–ocean temperature anomalies, 1880–2025. The dashed line marks the 1951–1980 reference level."}
ggplot(gistemp_df, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#888888",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_line(color = "#24476B", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(seq(1880, 2020, 20), "-01-01")),
    date_labels = "%Y",
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02))
  ) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Temperature anomaly (°C)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      color = "#E8E8E8",
      linewidth = 0.2
    ),
    panel.border = element_rect(
      color = "#888888",
      linewidth = 0.3
    )
  )
```

The series shows a long-term increase interrupted by substantial
monthly fluctuations. Warming is uneven: a relatively flat period
around the middle of the twentieth century is followed by a more
pronounced rise from approximately the 1970s onward. Recent
observations remain above the reference level.

# Persistence and Variability

We examine autocorrelation up to 48 months and the standard
deviation within centered 120-month windows.

```{r persistence-variability, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=2.4, out.width="95%", fig.pos="H", fig.cap="Autocorrelation of monthly anomalies (A) and rolling standard deviation over centered 120-month windows (B). Dashed ACF bands are approximate white-noise reference bounds."}
acf_values <- acf(gistemp_ts, lag.max = 48, plot = FALSE)

acf_df <- data.frame(
  lag = round(as.numeric(acf_values$lag) * frequency(gistemp_ts)),
  correlation = as.numeric(acf_values$acf)
)

acf_df <- acf_df[acf_df$lag > 0, ]
acf_bound <- qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(length(gistemp_ts))

rolling_df <- data.frame(
  date = gistemp_df$date,
  sd = as.numeric(zoo::rollapply(
    gistemp_ts,
    width = 120,
    FUN = sd,
    align = "center",
    fill = NA
  ))
)

diagnostic_theme <- theme_bw(base_size = 8) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 9, face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_rect(
      color = "#888888", linewidth = 0.3
    )
  )

p_acf <- ggplot(acf_df, aes(x = lag, y = correlation)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = c(-acf_bound, acf_bound),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#888888",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(xend = lag, yend = 0),
    color = "#24476B",
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 48, 12)) +
  labs(title = "A  Autocorrelation", x = "Lag (months)", y = "ACF") +
  diagnostic_theme

p_sd <- ggplot(rolling_df, aes(x = date, y = sd)) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#24476B",
    linewidth = 0.35,
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(seq(1900, 2020, 40), "-01-01")),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "B  Rolling standard deviation",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Standard deviation (°C)"
  ) +
  diagnostic_theme

diagnostic_grobs <- lapply(list(p_acf, p_sd), ggplotGrob)

common_heights <- do.call(
  grid::unit.pmax,
  lapply(diagnostic_grobs, function(g) g$heights)
)

grid::grid.newpage()
grid::pushViewport(
  grid::viewport(layout = grid::grid.layout(1, 2))
)

for (i in seq_along(diagnostic_grobs)) {
  diagnostic_grobs[[i]]$heights <- common_heights
  grid::pushViewport(
    grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = i)
  )
  grid::grid.draw(diagnostic_grobs[[i]])
  grid::popViewport()
}

grid::popViewport()
```

Autocorrelations remain high across the displayed lags, indicating
strong persistence consistent with the long-term movement.
This is not a formal test of non-stationarity.

The rolling standard deviation varies over time without a steady
increase across the full sample. Since each window also contains
local trend movements, this measure does not isolate the variance
of the irregular component.

# Classical Decomposition

We compare additive decomposition, $Y_t = T_t + S_t + R_t$,
with multiplicative decomposition, $Y_t = T_t S_t R_t$.
Both estimate the trend using centered moving averages and impose
a repeating seasonal pattern.

Temperature anomalies include negative values and cross zero,
making proportional seasonal factors difficult to interpret.
The multiplicative specification is retained as a diagnostic comparison.

```{r classical-decomposition-data, include=FALSE}
dec_add <- decompose(gistemp_ts, type = "additive")
dec_mult <- decompose(gistemp_ts, type = "multiplicative")

make_dec_df <- function(fit) {
  result <- pivot_longer(
    data.frame(
      date = gistemp_df$date,
      Observed = as.numeric(fit$x),
      Trend = as.numeric(fit$trend),
      Seasonal = as.numeric(fit$seasonal),
      Remainder = as.numeric(fit$random)
    ),
    cols = -date,
    names_to = "component",
    values_to = "value"
  )

  result$component <- factor(
    result$component,
    levels = c("Observed", "Trend", "Seasonal", "Remainder")
  )

  result
}

dec_add_df <- make_dec_df(dec_add)
dec_mult_df <- make_dec_df(dec_mult)
```

```{r classical-decomposition-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=4, out.width="90%", fig.pos="H", fig.cap="Classical additive (A) and multiplicative (B) decompositions. Vertical scales vary across panels. Additive components are in degrees Celsius; multiplicative seasonal and remainder components are ratios."}
climate_dec_plot <- function(data, title) {
  ggplot(data, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
    geom_line(
      color = "#243746",
      linewidth = 0.25,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ) +
    facet_wrap(~component, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_x_date(
      breaks = as.Date(paste0(c(1900, 1950, 2000), "-01-01")),
      date_labels = "%Y"
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(n = 3)
    ) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_bw(base_size = 8) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(
        size = 9, face = "bold", hjust = 0
      ),
      strip.background = element_rect(
        fill = "#F2F2F2", color = NA
      ),
      strip.text = element_text(size = 8),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
        color = "#E8E8E8", linewidth = 0.2
      ),
      panel.border = element_rect(
        color = "#888888", linewidth = 0.3
      ),
      panel.spacing = grid::unit(0.6, "lines"),
      axis.text = element_text(size = 7, color = "#333333"),
      plot.margin = margin(4, 6, 4, 4)
    )
}

dec_plots <- list(
  climate_dec_plot(dec_add_df, "A  Additive"),
  climate_dec_plot(dec_mult_df, "B  Multiplicative")
)

dec_grobs <- lapply(dec_plots, ggplotGrob)

common_widths <- do.call(
  grid::unit.pmax,
  lapply(dec_grobs, function(g) g$widths)
)

common_heights <- do.call(
  grid::unit.pmax,
  lapply(dec_grobs, function(g) g$heights)
)

grid::grid.newpage()
grid::pushViewport(
  grid::viewport(layout = grid::grid.layout(1, 2))
)

for (i in seq_along(dec_grobs)) {
  dec_grobs[[i]]$widths <- common_widths
  dec_grobs[[i]]$heights <- common_heights

  grid::pushViewport(
    grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = i)
  )
  grid::grid.draw(dec_grobs[[i]])
  grid::popViewport()
}

grid::popViewport()
```

The trend estimates coincide because both specifications use the
same moving-average filter. They show an uneven long-term increase,
with stronger warming in the later decades.

The multiplicative remainder exhibits extreme spikes when its
denominator, the product of trend and seasonal components, approaches
zero. These ratios are sensitive to the chosen anomaly baseline.
We therefore use an additive representation for subsequent analysis.
The additive remainder still requires examination; its appearance
alone does not establish white noise.

# Fixed and Time-Varying Seasonality

We compare robust STL with a fixed annual seasonal pattern
(`s.window = "periodic"`) and a pattern allowed to evolve over time
(`s.window = 13`). Robust fitting reduces the influence of unusually
large remainder values.

```{r stl-comparison-data, include=FALSE}
stl_periodic <- stl(
  gistemp_ts,
  s.window = "periodic",
  robust = TRUE
)

stl_varying <- stl(
  gistemp_ts,
  s.window = 13,
  robust = TRUE
)

make_stl_df <- function(fit, specification) {
  pivot_longer(
    data.frame(
      date = gistemp_df$date,
      Observed = as.numeric(gistemp_ts),
      Trend = as.numeric(fit$time.series[, "trend"]),
      Seasonal = as.numeric(fit$time.series[, "seasonal"]),
      Remainder = as.numeric(fit$time.series[, "remainder"])
    ),
    cols = -date,
    names_to = "component",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
    mutate(specification = specification)
}

stl_comparison <- bind_rows(
  make_stl_df(stl_periodic, "A  Fixed seasonality"),
  make_stl_df(stl_varying, "B  Time-varying seasonality")
)

stl_comparison$component <- factor(
  stl_comparison$component,
  levels = c("Observed", "Trend", "Seasonal", "Remainder")
)
```

```{r stl-comparison-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=4, out.width="90%", fig.pos="H", fig.cap="Robust STL with fixed (A) and time-varying (B) seasonality. Components are expressed in degrees Celsius. Each row shares a vertical scale across the two specifications."}
ggplot(stl_comparison, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
  geom_line(color = "#243746", linewidth = 0.25) +
  facet_grid(
    component ~ specification,
    scales = "free_y"
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(c(1900, 1950, 2000), "-01-01")),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(n = 3)
  ) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 8) +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#F2F2F2", color = NA
    ),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 8),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      color = "#E8E8E8", linewidth = 0.2
    ),
    panel.border = element_rect(
      color = "#888888", linewidth = 0.3
    ),
    panel.spacing = grid::unit(0.6, "lines"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 7, color = "#333333")
  )
```

Both specifications recover a similar long-term warming pattern.
The flexible specification allocates more variation to the seasonal
component, but this alone does not establish that the variation
represents a stable seasonal signal.

We retain fixed seasonality as a parsimonious working specification
for forecasting. This is a modelling choice, rather than evidence
that seasonality is constant or that the flexible fit overfits.

# Seasonal Pattern and Remainder

We examine the monthly seasonal effects and the remainder from
classical additive decomposition.

```{r seasonal-remainder-data, include=FALSE}
seasonal_df <- data.frame(
  month = factor(month.abb, levels = month.abb),
  value = as.numeric(dec_add$figure)
)

remainder_df <- data.frame(
  date = gistemp_df$date,
  value = as.numeric(dec_add$random)
)
```

```{r seasonal-remainder-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=2, out.width="95%", fig.pos="H", fig.cap="Monthly seasonal effects (A) and remainder over time (B) from classical additive decomposition, in degrees Celsius."}
p_seasonal <- ggplot(seasonal_df, aes(x = month, y = value)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#24476B", width = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    color = "#888888",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "A  Monthly seasonal effects",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Seasonal effect (°C)"
  ) +
  diagnostic_theme +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 6))

p_remainder <- ggplot(remainder_df, aes(x = date, y = value)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    color = "#888888",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_line(
    color = "#24476B",
    linewidth = 0.25,
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(c(1900, 1950, 2000), "-01-01")),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "B  Remainder",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Remainder (°C)"
  ) +
  diagnostic_theme

seasonal_grobs <- lapply(
  list(p_seasonal, p_remainder),
  ggplotGrob
)

common_heights <- do.call(
  grid::unit.pmax,
  lapply(seasonal_grobs, function(g) g$heights)
)

grid::grid.newpage()
grid::pushViewport(
  grid::viewport(layout = grid::grid.layout(1, 2))
)

for (i in seq_along(seasonal_grobs)) {
  seasonal_grobs[[i]]$heights <- common_heights

  grid::pushViewport(
    grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = i)
  )
  grid::grid.draw(seasonal_grobs[[i]])
  grid::popViewport()
}

grid::popViewport()
```

The estimated monthly effects are small, with positive peaks
in March and October and negative effects in several summer
and winter months. These are patterns in temperature anomalies,
not the annual cycle of absolute temperatures; their physical
causes cannot be inferred from this decomposition.

The remainder fluctuates around zero with occasional large
deviations, particularly early in the record. These represent
variation left unexplained by the estimated trend and fixed
seasonal pattern.

# Exponential Smoothing

We seasonally adjust the January 1950–December 2010 sample using
robust periodic STL fitted to that sample only. We then compare
simple exponential smoothing (SES), which updates a level,
with Holt's method, which also updates a trend.

```{r smoothing-models, include=FALSE}
train_raw <- window(
  gistemp_ts,
  start = c(1950, 1),
  end = c(2010, 12)
)

stl_train <- stl(
  train_raw,
  s.window = "periodic",
  robust = TRUE
)

deseas_sub <- train_raw - stl_train$time.series[, "seasonal"]

ses_fit <- HoltWinters(
  deseas_sub,
  beta = FALSE,
  gamma = FALSE
)

hw_fit <- HoltWinters(
  deseas_sub,
  beta = NULL,
  gamma = FALSE
)

smoothing_models <- list(
  "A  SES" = ses_fit,
  "B  Holt" = hw_fit
)

smoothing_observed <- data.frame(
  date = as.Date(as.yearmon(time(deseas_sub))),
  value = as.numeric(deseas_sub)
)

smoothing_fitted <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(smoothing_models), function(model_name) {
    fit <- smoothing_models[[model_name]]

    data.frame(
      date = as.Date(as.yearmon(time(fit$fitted))),
      value = as.numeric(fit$fitted[, "xhat"]),
      model = model_name
    )
  })
)
```

```{r smoothing-comparison, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=3, out.width="90%", fig.pos="H", fig.cap="Seasonally adjusted training observations and one-step-ahead fitted values from SES and Holt, 1950–2010. Both panels share the same axes."}
ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = smoothing_observed,
    aes(x = date, y = value, color = "Observed"),
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = smoothing_fitted,
    aes(x = date, y = value, color = "One-step fitted"),
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~model, ncol = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Observed" = "#555555",
      "One-step fitted" = "#B36B35"
    ),
    breaks = c("Observed", "One-step fitted")
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(c(1950, 1970, 1990, 2010), "-01-01")),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Adjusted anomaly (°C)",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#F2F2F2", color = NA
    ),
    strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8)
  )
```

The estimated level smoothing parameters are
$\alpha = `r sprintf("%.3f", ses_fit$alpha)`$ for SES and
$\alpha = `r sprintf("%.3f", hw_fit$alpha)`$ for Holt.
Holt's trend smoothing parameter is
$\beta = `r sprintf("%.3f", hw_fit$beta)`$.
Parameters are selected by minimizing the in-sample sum of squared
one-step-ahead errors.

These fitted values use preceding observations, but their smoothing
parameters and seasonal adjustment are estimated from the full
training sample. Their fit therefore does not establish performance
on unseen data.

We next fix Holt's level smoothing parameter at 0.1 and 0.9,
re-estimating the trend smoothing parameter in each case.

```{r alpha-sensitivity-data, include=FALSE}
holt_low <- HoltWinters(
  deseas_sub, alpha = 0.1, beta = NULL, gamma = FALSE
)

holt_high <- HoltWinters(
  deseas_sub, alpha = 0.9, beta = NULL, gamma = FALSE
)

alpha_models <- list(
  "A  Alpha = 0.1" = holt_low,
  "B  Alpha = 0.9" = holt_high
)

alpha_fitted <- bind_rows(
  lapply(names(alpha_models), function(model_name) {
    fit <- alpha_models[[model_name]]

    data.frame(
      date = as.Date(as.yearmon(time(fit$fitted))),
      value = as.numeric(fit$fitted[, "xhat"]),
      model = model_name
    )
  })
)
```

```{r alpha-sensitivity-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=3, out.width="90%", fig.pos="H", fig.cap="Holt one-step-ahead fitted values with alpha fixed at 0.1 and 0.9. Beta is estimated separately for each specification; both panels share the same axes."}
ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = smoothing_observed,
    aes(x = date, y = value, color = "Observed"),
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = alpha_fitted,
    aes(x = date, y = value, color = "One-step fitted"),
    linewidth = 0.35
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~model, ncol = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Observed" = "#555555",
      "One-step fitted" = "#B36B35"
    ),
    breaks = c("Observed", "One-step fitted")
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(paste0(c(1950, 1970, 1990, 2010), "-01-01")),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Adjusted anomaly (°C)",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#F2F2F2", color = NA
    ),
    strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8)
  )
```

A larger alpha gives the latest observation greater weight in the
level update. The comparison also reflects the separately estimated
beta values: `r sprintf("%.3f", holt_low$beta)` for alpha = 0.1 and
`r sprintf("%.3f", holt_high$beta)` for alpha = 0.9.
Responsiveness alone does not establish better forecast accuracy.

# Forecast Evaluation

The Holt model estimated on the seasonally adjusted 1950–2010 sample
produces forecasts for January 2011 through December 2025, without
re-estimation. Test observations are adjusted using the monthly seasonal
effects estimated on the training sample.

```{r forecast-data, include=FALSE}
test_raw <- window(
  gistemp_ts,
  start = c(2011, 1),
  end = c(2025, 12)
)

training_seasonal_effects <- tapply(
  stl_train$time.series[, "seasonal"],
  cycle(train_raw),
  mean
)

test_adjusted <- ts(
  as.numeric(test_raw) -
    training_seasonal_effects[cycle(test_raw)],
  start = start(test_raw),
  frequency = frequency(test_raw)
)

holt_fc <- forecast::forecast(
  hw_fit,
  h = length(test_adjusted),
  level = c(80, 95)
)

stopifnot(
  length(test_adjusted) == 180L,
  all(is.finite(test_adjusted)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    as.numeric(time(test_adjusted)),
    as.numeric(time(holt_fc$mean))
  ))
)

forecast_df <- data.frame(
  date = as.Date(as.yearmon(time(holt_fc$mean))),
  mean = as.numeric(holt_fc$mean),
  lower80 = as.numeric(holt_fc$lower[, "80%"]),
  upper80 = as.numeric(holt_fc$upper[, "80%"]),
  lower95 = as.numeric(holt_fc$lower[, "95%"]),
  upper95 = as.numeric(holt_fc$upper[, "95%"])
)

observed_df <- data.frame(
  date = c(
    as.Date(as.yearmon(time(deseas_sub))),
    as.Date(as.yearmon(time(test_adjusted)))
  ),
  value = c(
    as.numeric(deseas_sub),
    as.numeric(test_adjusted)
  )
)
```

```{r forecast-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.4, fig.height=3, out.width="95%", fig.pos="H", fig.cap="Holt forecasts from the end of 2010, with 80% and 95% prediction intervals. Observations are seasonally adjusted using training-sample estimates. The dashed line marks the start of the test period. Intervals are conditional on the fitted model and exclude uncertainty in seasonal adjustment."}
ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = forecast_df,
    aes(x = date, ymin = lower95, ymax = upper95),
    fill = "#24476B",
    alpha = 0.12
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = forecast_df,
    aes(x = date, ymin = lower80, ymax = upper80),
    fill = "#24476B",
    alpha = 0.22
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = observed_df,
    aes(x = date, y = value, color = "Observed"),
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = forecast_df,
    aes(x = date, y = mean, color = "Forecast"),
    linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = as.numeric(as.Date("2011-01-01")),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "#888888",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Observed" = "#555555",
      "Forecast" = "#24476B"
    ),
    breaks = c("Observed", "Forecast"),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = as.Date(c(
      "1950-01-01", "1970-01-01",
      "1990-01-01", "2010-01-01", "2025-01-01"
    )),
    date_labels = "%Y"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Adjusted anomaly (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8)
  )
```
The point forecasts extend the estimated trend, while observations
in the later test years generally lie above the forecast path.
Prediction intervals widen substantially over the fifteen-year horizon.

Forecast accuracy is summarized using mean absolute error (MAE)
over the first 12, 60, 120, and 180 test months. Each value averages
all monthly absolute errors up to the indicated horizon; it is not
the error at the endpoint alone.

```{r forecast-mae, echo=FALSE}
forecast_errors <- (
  as.numeric(test_adjusted) -
    as.numeric(holt_fc$mean)
)

horizons <- c(12L, 60L, 120L, 180L)

mae_results <- data.frame(
  Horizon = c("1 year", "5 years", "10 years", "15 years"),
  Months = horizons,
  MAE = vapply(
    horizons,
    function(h) {
      mean(abs(forecast_errors[seq_len(h)]))
    },
    numeric(1)
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  mae_results,
  col.names = c("Evaluation horizon", "Months", "MAE (°C)"),
  digits = 3,
  row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Cumulative forecast MAE from January 2011."
)
```
Cumulative MAE increases from 0.120 °C over the first year to
0.239 °C over fifteen years. Average absolute errors are therefore
higher when later test observations are included. These results
describe a single forecast origin and do not establish how accuracy
would vary across different estimation periods.

# Discussion and Limitations

Additive decomposition is appropriate for temperature anomalies,
which include negative and near-zero values. STL illustrates how
allowing seasonal effects to vary changes the allocation between
seasonality and remainder. The Holt forecasts extend the estimated
trend but generally underpredict anomalies in the later test years.

The evaluation uses one chronological split and a dataset retrieved
after the forecast origin, rather than the data vintage available
in 2010. Prediction intervals depend on the model assumptions and
exclude uncertainty in seasonal adjustment. The analysis provides
a statistical description and forecasting illustration, without
identifying the causes of temperature changes.
